analysis.one_liner: Sets federal data-security standards for companies holding personal information and requires them to tell people when their data is breached.
analysis.headline: The House passed the data security and breach notification bill by voice vote in December 2009, but it died in a Senate committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring any company that holds Americans' personal information to keep it secure, and to tell affected people and the FTC within 60 days when that data is breached. Companies would have had to offer free credit monitoring or credit reports for two years after a breach. Special rules targeted "information brokers" — companies that buy and sell people's personal data — requiring them to let individuals see and correct their records, and banning them from getting information by deception. The bill also preempted some stronger state laws on the same subject. The House passed it in December 2009, but the Senate never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose personal information companies hold: the bill would have forced companies to adopt security policies, notify them of breaches within 60 days, and provide free credit monitoring or credit reports after a breach. It also would have given people the right to review and correct the data brokers keep on them and to stop brokers selling their information for marketing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose data is held online

how_it_helps.text: Requires any company holding Americans' personal data to follow FTC-set security policies, including vulnerability testing and secure disposal of old records.

Requires notification to affected individuals and the FTC within 60 days of a breach, and requires the breached company to provide affected people free credit reports or credit monitoring for two years.
Gives individuals the right to review and correct the personal information that data brokers keep on them, and to opt out of having it sold for marketing.
Makes it illegal for information brokers to obtain personal information by false pretenses (pretexting), and authorizes state attorneys general to sue violators for penalties up to $5 million.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect and hold personal data, which would bear the cost of security programs, breach notification, audits, and two years of credit monitoring for breach victims — costs likely passed to consumers in prices. Data brokers face the heaviest new requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state information security and breach-notification laws, which would replace stronger state rules in states like California with a single federal standard — a tradeoff consumer groups have long criticized in federal data-breach bills.

Companies are exempt from telling anyone about a breach if they determine there is no reasonable risk of identity theft or fraud, and encrypted data triggers a presumption of no risk — leaving the company, not the victim, to make that judgment.

The bill bars individuals from suing over violations of its security and notification provisions; enforcement is left to the FTC and state attorneys general, and state AG penalties are capped at $5 million per violation type.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — mandatory data safeguards, breach notification, free credit monitoring, and accuracy rights for information held by brokers — are real and would have helped consumers at modest cost to companies that hold data. The honest caveats: the breach-notification exemption and encryption safe harbor give companies a way to avoid telling people their data was compromised, and the preemption of stricter state laws would replace a patchwork of stronger state rules (like California's) with a single federal floor. Whether that trade was good depended heavily on FTC rules that were never written, because the bill never became law.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote, but it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on December 8, 2009 by voice vote under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure usually reserved for noncontroversial bills.

The Senate received the bill on December 9, 2009 and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding personal data continued operating under only the patchwork of state breach laws, with no federal security standards or FTC audit regime. Data brokers were better off that the bill died; consumers gained nothing from its passage.

sides.party_line_note: The House passed it by voice vote with a sponsor and cosponsors from both parties, so no recorded party split exists; the Senate never voted, leaving no roll-call record of opposition.

industries.note: New security, audit, accuracy, and consumer-access obligations would directly constrain a business built on collecting and selling personal data, and pretexting would become explicitly illegal. But the bill also entrenches the industry: instead of eliminating or restructuring data brokerage, it legitimizes the practice under federal rules and, by preempting state laws, would prevent states from imposing stricter regimes. The bill died, so none of this took effect.

industries.industry: Credit reporting agencies and credit monitoring firms
industries.note: Every large breach would funnel millions of breach victims into free credit reports and credit monitoring for two years, a steady stream of business for monitoring services; the bill also requires companies to coordinate with the major credit bureaus. Consumers get a protection that conveniently runs through the credit industry's own products rather than, say, mandatory data minimization.

industries.industry: Any company holding consumer data (retailers, banks, online services)
industries.note: Would face mandatory security programs, 60-day breach notification duties, and FTC and state AG enforcement with multi-million dollar penalties. Ordinary people bear less of the cost of identity theft as a result.
